newsitem.title: GREECE: Ecologists slam Athens' 2004 Olympic bid.
newsitem.headline: Ecologists slam Athens' 2004 Olympic bid.

text.p: Greek environmentalists on Tuesday slammed Athens's bid to host the 2004 summer Olympics, saying its proposals spelled ecological disaster instead of improving the capital's image.
The city's bid proposals to the International Olympic Committee (IOC) fail to assess any damage to the environment or long-term effect on life there, the international group Greenpeace said.

"Not only is the enviromental impact of the Games disregarded but the basic principles of the Athens city plan are violated," Ilias Efthymiopoulos, head of Greenpeace's Greek office told a news conference.
Other environmental groups have also criticised the choice of venues for several sports, as well as the bidding committee's failure to consult with them before submitting its proposals.

"The committee lies in the bidding dossier by saying that it has already contacted environmental groups. If it had done that, serious mistakes would have been avoided," Greece's Ornithological Society said in a statement.
The Athens bidding committee declined comment.

Athens is among 11 candidate cities to host the 2004 Games and is considered among the top favourites along with Cape Town, Stockholm and Rome. The IOC will short-list four or five cities in March, before making their final choice in September.
Environmental groups say one of the most environmentally offensive plans are a rowing and canoeing venue at the sensitive bird habitat of Skinias north east of Athens.
"Skinias is the most important seaside habitat of the Attica region and has been included in various European Union preservation programmes," the Ornithological Society said.
Greenpeace also criticised the choice of venue for an Olympic village, at the foot of mount Parnes north of Athens.
"Have the effects of moving ozone pollution to the area been assessed? What will it mean for Athens to have a 40,000-resident town built at the foot of the mountain?" Efthymiopoulos asked.
The groups said there was still time to discuss improving the Athens dossier, which could mean the revamping of the sprawling city of four million people instead of its further deterioration.
"Barcelona did it," Efthymiopoulos said. "The Olympics could be a chance for Athens to promote its cultural identity and upgrade its tourism."

After losing the centennial 1996 Games to Atlanta, Athens had vowed never to bid again but soon changed its mind and decided to vie for the 2004 Olympics by projecting an image of a modern city with state of the art facilities.
